title: Content with right action
hookLine: the mind is content with itself when it acts rightly (Meditations 7.28)

cards: You return a wallet you found on the sidewalk. Nobody's watching. No reward, no thank-you note, no story to tell at dinner; the owner never even learns your name.
And yet you walk away a little lighter. Something in you settles, like a picture hanging straight. Where does that feeling come from, when nothing outside you changed?
Marcus Aurelius had an answer, and it's a very short entry in book seven.

teach.b: Meditations seven, twenty-eight, begins, in George Long's translation: "Retire into thyself." Go inward, not to hide, but to check what's there.
Marcus says the ruling part of the mind, what the Stoics called the hegemonikon, is content with itself when it does what's just, and that brings it calm. That's the whole entry.
Notice what's missing: no applause, no result. The mind's contentment doesn't depend on whether the wallet's owner is grateful, or whether anyone knows. It comes from the act itself.

If your peace depends on outcomes, you're always waiting: for thanks, for the plan to work, for people to notice. Marcus points to a satisfaction fully in your control. You can't make the world reward you.

teach.h: NOT SMUG: A KEY IN A LOCK.
teach.b: You can do the right thing, and the mind, he says, is built to be content with that.
A fair caution: some hear this as smugness, being pleased with yourself for being good. Not quite.
Elsewhere Marcus warns against wanting credit even from yourself, comparing the good person to a vine that bears grapes and asks for nothing. The contentment here is quieter.
Less a pat on the back, more the click of a key turning in the right lock.

how: Readers of Marcus often notice the quiet satisfaction of doing something right that nobody sees, and treat it as enough, rather than waiting for thanks or results.

o: Marcus's image for doing good without asking for credit
a sign of wealth, grapes paid back as a reward for good
a symbol of the wine Romans drank at their feasts

games.q: content with right action — tap the pairs.
p: the ruling part of the mind

s: Marcus says the ruling mind is content when it acts justly
and that this brings it calm, whatever the outcome.
Marcus says the contentment comes from being praised
it comes from the act itself; praise isn't part of it.

games.q: you did the right thing, and nobody thanked you or even noticed. by 7.28, what's left?
o: the mind's own contentment in having acted rightly.
games.why: Meditations 7.28: the ruling principle is content with itself when it does what is just, and so finds calm.

practice: Remember one right thing you did recently that nobody noticed: a dish that wasn't yours, the truth when a lie was easier, patience on the phone. Let the memory settle, without inflating it or dismissing it.
If there's a quiet rightness in it, let yourself enjoy it, the way you'd enjoy warm sun.

wordCard.voice: Vine. Marcus's image for the good person: a vine that bears grapes and asks for nothing. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the ruling part, the Stoic word for the mind's command center, which Marcus refers to in 7.28.

carryVoice: Your line: content with right. No applause needed; the act is enough. Until next time.
